recall.define: Without the glossary, define exception (Arm), interrupt (Arm), interrupt handler, NVIC, Thread mode, Handler mode and exception priority, and say which document defines each.
recall.distinguish: State the difference and the observable consequence for each pair: exception versus interrupt; preemption priority versus subpriority; tail-chaining versus late arrival; interrupt latency versus response time; hardware barrier versus compiler barrier.
recall.apply: A DMA completion handler hands a buffer to a thread through a ring. Using the terms exception entry and return, interrupt latency, DMA transfer and cache maintenance, explain which events bound the time from the hardware event to the thread's read, where PRIMASK masking would lengthen it, and which term names the hazard if the Cortex-M7 data cache is not cleaned before the DMA starts.

entries.definition: An Armv7-M architectural transfer to exception handling, including reset, NMI, faults, SVCall, PendSV, SysTick and external interrupts. Interrupts are a subset of exceptions; the architecture also calls PendSV and SysTick system-level interrupts. Their architectural behavior is distinct from a language exception mechanism.

authority.locator: pp.42-44 section2.3.7 exception entry/return and frame

distinguish_from.distinction: A POSIX signal is software delivered by the kernel; an Arm exception is a hardware control transfer with its own stacking and priority rules.

idiom: the exception number indexes the vector table
a fault exception escalates to HardFault
entries.misconception: Exceptions on Cortex-M are error conditions (SysTick and PendSV are ordinary exceptions).

entries.definition: An asynchronous exception request subject to the Armv7-M exception priority and masking rules. External interrupts have exception numbers16 and above and NVIC enable/pending controls. PendSV and SysTick are system-level interrupts with separate control bits; defining every interrupt as an external peripheral request excludes these cases.
idiom: enable the interrupt in the NVIC and in the peripheral
entries.misconception: Enabling the peripheral's interrupt bit is enough (the NVIC enable and priority are separate).

entries.definition: The function whose address sits in the vector table entry for an interrupt and that the processor enters in Handler mode, with the AAPCS caller-saved registers stacked by hardware; written as an ordinary C function. 'ISR' is the common abbreviation (interrupt service routine).

authority.locator: pp.42-44 section2.3.7 exception entry/return and frame

distinguish_from.distinction: An exception handler serves any exception, including faults and SysTick; an interrupt handler serves a peripheral interrupt. The hardware treats them identically.

idiom: keep the handler short and defer work to a thread
entries.misconception: An interrupt handler needs a special calling convention or assembly wrapper on Cortex-M (hardware stacking makes it an ordinary function).

entries.definition: The Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller manages external interrupt enable, pending, active and priority state. Disabling an interrupt does not clear pending or active state, and clearing pending does not acknowledge a still-asserted peripheral source. Multiple pulses can coalesce into one pending event. Strict exercises program inspected registers directly; CMSIS convenience APIs are not target dependencies.
entries.misconception: The NVIC is part of the peripheral (it is part of the processor core).

entries.definition: An Armv7-M table whose entry0 supplies the initial main stack pointer and whose exception-number entries supply handler addresses. Handler entries require the Thumb-state bit; base address on reset is implementation-defined and VTOR supports relocation. Required power-of-two alignment depends on the supported exception count, with a128-byte minimum, not a universal128-byte sufficient alignment.
entries.misconception: The vector table must be at address zero (it must be where VTOR points; zero is only the reset default alias).

entries.definition: The processor mode in which application code runs, entered at reset and on return from the last active exception; it can use either stack pointer and may be privileged or unprivileged according to the CONTROL register.
entries.misconception: Thread mode means an RTOS thread is running (it is a hardware mode, present without any operating system).

entries.definition: The processor mode entered when an exception is taken; it is always privileged and always uses the main stack pointer, and the IPSR holds the active exception number.
entries.misconception: A handler can run on the process stack (it always uses MSP).

entries.definition: Armv7-M urgency uses lower numerical values for higher priority. Reset, NMI and HardFault have fixed priorities -3, -2 and -1. Configurable fields use implemented high-order bits; group priority, active exceptions and mask registers determine preemption. Subpriority and exception number arbitrate ties without independently enabling preemption.
idiom: lower numeric priority value means higher urgency
entries.misconception: Priority 255 is the most urgent.

entries.definition: The group of priority bits, selected by the priority grouping field, that decides whether one exception can preempt another; the remaining bits form the subpriority, which only orders exceptions that are pending simultaneously and never causes preemption.
entries.misconception: Any difference in priority allows preemption (only a difference in the preemption bits does).

entries.definition: A software-pended system exception with configurable priority. RTOS designs commonly assign it the lowest group priority for deferred context switching; the architecture does not force that assignment. At reset configurable priorities are zero. Whether it can preempt another handler follows the configured grouping, priorities and masks.
entries.misconception: PendSV switches context by itself (it only provides the safe place to do so).

entries.definition: An Armv7-M downcounter with a24-bit reload field. With TICKINT enabled, counting to zero makes SysTick pending; reload occurs on the following timer clock. COUNTFLAG records a transition rather than an accumulated count, and a software write clearing CURRENT does not itself pend the exception. Clock choice, debug behavior and initialization matter.
entries.misconception: SysTick is an STM32 peripheral (it is an Arm core feature).

entries.definition: The synchronous supervisor-call exception generated by SVC. An operating system may use it to enter a privileged service handler. Interpreting the instruction immediate as a service number is an OS ABI convention; C and the exception mechanism do not supply that dispatch contract automatically.
entries.misconception: SVC is an interrupt (it is a synchronous exception).

entries.definition: An Armv7-M fault exception at fixed priority -1, below Reset and NMI and above configurable exceptions. It handles escalated faults and some directly reported failures such as vector-table read errors. HFSR and applicable configurable fault status help distinguish them; HardFault is not a configurable-priority exception and does not guarantee recoverability.

distinguish_from.distinction: On Linux the kernel converts the fault into a signal; on the bare-metal board the handler is the final observer and must record the fault itself.

entries.misconception: A HardFault means a hardware defect.

entries.definition: The hardware sequence that stacks r0–r3, r12, lr, pc and xPSR (plus floating-point registers when lazy stacking is not used), loads lr with an EXC_RETURN value encoding the stack and mode to resume, and restores the frame when the handler returns through that value.

authority.locator: pp.42-44 section2.3.7 exception entry/return and frame

entries.misconception: The handler must save all registers (the hardware saves the caller-saved set; the handler, as a C function, saves what it uses).

entries.definition: The optimization by which the processor enters a pending exception directly from the returning handler without unstacking and restacking the frame, shortening back-to-back handler latency.

authority.locator: B1.5.12, pp.B1-548–549, prose and TailChain entry

distinguish_from.distinction: Late arrival lets a higher-priority exception that arrives during stacking take precedence before the first handler starts; tail-chaining joins handlers at return.

entries.misconception: Tail-chaining changes the priority order (it only removes redundant stacking).

entries.definition: An implementation-supported optimization in which a higher-priority exception arriving during exception entry uses the entry sequence already in progress. The original exception stays pending. The architecture constrains the priority relation but leaves recognition conditions implementation-defined; a universal cycle saving cannot be inferred from the mechanism.
entries.misconception: Once stacking has begun the first exception always runs first.

entries.definition: The time from the interrupt request being asserted to the first instruction of its handler; it includes the hardware stacking cycles, any time the interrupt is masked (PRIMASK, BASEPRI, FAULTMASK) and any higher-priority handler already running. Response time adds the handler's own work.

authority.locator: C1.8.3 CYCCNT cycle counter and related timers — CYCCNT definition and profiling notes

distinguish_from.distinction: Latency ends when the handler starts; response time ends when the required reaction is complete.

idiom: measure interrupt latency with a GPIO toggle on the logic analyzer
entries.misconception: Interrupt latency is a fixed number from the datasheet (masking and nesting make it workload-dependent).

entries.definition: Temporarily preventing exception entry: PRIMASK blocks all configurable exceptions, BASEPRI blocks those at or below a priority, FAULTMASK blocks everything but NMI. A critical section built this way lengthens interrupt latency by its duration.
entries.misconception: Disabling interrupts makes shared data safe on a multicore device (masking is per core).

entries.definition: The two banked stack pointers of Armv7-M: the main stack pointer used by handlers and by Thread mode at reset, and the process stack pointer an operating system gives to threads so that handler stacking never overruns a thread's stack. CONTROL.SPSEL selects which one Thread mode uses.
entries.misconception: There is one stack on a Cortex-M.

entries.definition: Data movement by a controller under a device-specific address, direction, width and completion contract. Software must preserve each borrowed buffer and avoid conflicting accesses while ownership is with the device; disjoint buffers or immutable source reads require their own contract rather than a universal no-CPU-access rule. Cache maintenance depends on coherence and target. A stop request may precede completed transfer/FIFO draining.
entries.misconception: A DMA completion flag means the data is visible to the processor (on a cached core the cache may still hold stale lines).

entries.definition: A memory record in a hardware-defined format that tells a bus-master controller (DMA, Ethernet MAC) where a buffer is, how long it is and who owns it; the controller and the software hand ownership back and forth through a flag in the descriptor. Unrelated to a POSIX file descriptor.

distinguish_from.distinction: Same word, different world: the file descriptor is a kernel handle; the DMA descriptor is a hardware-owned memory record.

entries.misconception: The descriptor can be modified while the controller owns it.

entries.definition: The explicit clean (write back) and invalidate operations a Cortex-M7 program must issue on the data cache around DMA transfers and shared-memory handoffs, because the cache is not coherent with bus masters or the other core; done per cache line, which makes buffer alignment part of the contract.
entries.misconception: A memory barrier substitutes for cache maintenance.

entries.definition: A read-modify-write sequence can overwrite an intervening update, or write back side-effect status bits incorrectly. STM32F4 GPIO BSRR provides an atomic set/reset operation without reading ODR, but does not lock ODR against other writers. Use a mechanism valid for the register and all participating agents; CPU interrupt masking neither excludes DMA nor makes arbitrary MMIO suitable for C atomic operations.
idiom: use the BSRR set/clear register instead of a read-modify-write of ODR
entries.misconception: A single C statement like reg |= bit is atomic.
